{{DISPLAYTITLE:When Lean says no}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/System/Elaboration|Lean theorem prover/System/Metavariables and unification}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

A check that fails ends in a message. The message is not a mark of failure to be cleared
away; it says what Lean was trying to do and where it stopped. This page goes through the
refusals met most often and shows how to read each one. Every message quoted here is the one
Lean 4.34.1 prints for the code shown.

== Where a refusal comes from ==

Lean reads a source file in stages. It parses the text, then '''elaborates''' it: it turns
what the author wrote into terms of its core logic, filling in the details left out and
running the tactics. Then the Lean kernel checks each finished term against the rules of the
logic.<ref name="ref-elab">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0
(lean-lang.org, 2026), chapter 2, "Elaboration and Compilation", with section 2.3, "The
Kernel". https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/</ref> The
messages met day to day come from elaboration, which still knows what the author wrote and
can report in those terms. The Lean kernel's own check is there to guard against mistakes in
elaboration itself.<ref name="ref-elab" />

Each message is attached to a place in the file, given as line and column, and has a
severity: an error means that the definition or theorem was not accepted as written; a warning
does not. An editor connected to Lean underlines the place and shows the text.

== A value of the wrong type ==

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def three : Nat := "three"
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
Type mismatch
  "three"
has type
  String
but is expected to have type
  Nat
</pre>

The message has three parts: what was given, the type it has, and the type that was needed.
Here a piece of text was given where a number was promised. In a proof the same message
means that the proof offered proves a different statement from the one asked, since a
statement is the type of its proofs (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Types as specifications|types as specifications]]). The two
types side by side usually show where they part.

== Something left to prove ==

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem zero_add' (n : Nat) : 0 + n = n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ k ih => rw [Nat.add_succ]
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
unsolved goals
case succ
k : Nat
ih : 0 + k = k
⊢ (0 + k).succ = k + 1
</pre>

The tactics ran out with a goal still open, and Lean shows it in full: the hypotheses above
the line, what remains below it. Read this way the message nearly gives the answer. The
hypothesis <code>ih</code> says that 0 + k is k, and the goal contains 0 + k. Adding
<code>ih</code> to the rewrite finishes the proof, as on the page
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Induction, as the machine sees it|induction, as the machine
sees it]]. Goals and their display are described in
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Holes and goals|holes and goals]].

== No known way to do it ==

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
structure Colour where
  red : Nat
  green : Nat
  blue : Nat

def mix (a b : Colour) : Colour := a + b
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  HAdd Colour Colour ?m.3

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
</pre>

The sign + means different things for natural numbers, for integers and for other types. Lean finds
the right meaning by looking up an '''instance''': a definition, registered in advance, that
says how to add two values of given types. The message says that the lookup failed. Lean
looked for a way to add a <code>Colour</code> to a <code>Colour</code>, giving a result of a
type it had not yet settled, written <code>?m.3</code> (an unfilled hole, in the sense of
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Holes and goals|holes and goals]]), and found none, because
nobody has said what adding colours means. The message carries the name
<code>lean.synthInstanceFailed</code>, and the Lean Language Reference has an explanation
under that name. It notes that many such failures come from using the wrong operation, such
as <code>+</code> where <code>++</code>, which joins two pieces of text, was
meant.<ref name="ref-synth">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0
(lean-lang.org, 2026), "Error Explanations": <code>lean.synthInstanceFailed</code>.
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Error-Explanations/About___--synthInstanceFailed/</ref>

== No reason to stop ==

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def climb (n : Nat) : Nat :=
  if n = 0 then 0 else climb (n + 1)
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
fail to show termination for
  climb
with errors
failed to infer structural recursion:
Cannot use parameter n:
  failed to eliminate recursive application
    climb (n + 1)


failed to prove termination, possible solutions:
  - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
  - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
  - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
n : Nat
h✝ : ¬n = 0
⊢ n + 1 &lt; n
</pre>

Every function in Lean's logic must be shown to finish (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Functions that always finish|functions that always
finish]]). Lean tried two ways and reports both. Structural recursion failed because the
call is on n + 1, which is not a part of n. Well-founded recursion, with n itself as the
measure, failed too, and the last three lines show the obligation it could not meet: knowing that n is not 0, show that n + 1
is less than n. That is false. Here the message has found a real fault: for any n other than
0, the function would call itself for ever. When the obligation is true but Lean's default
search cannot prove it, the remedies listed in the message apply.<ref name="ref-rec">''The
Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0 (lean-lang.org, 2026), section 7.6,
"Recursive Definitions".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/</ref>

== A statement that is false ==

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example : 2 + 2 = 5 := by decide
</pre>

Lean answers <code>Tactic `decide` proved that the proposition</code> <code>2 + 2 = 5</code>
<code>is false</code>. This refusal is stronger than the others. The tactic
<code>decide</code> computes whether a statement is true, and here the computation came out
the other way, so the message is in effect a disproof.<ref name="ref-tacref">''The Lean
Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0 (lean-lang.org, 2026), section 14.5, "Tactic
Reference": entry for <code>decide</code>.
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/</ref> Most
refusals say less. An unsolved goal or a failed search says only that this attempt did not
succeed; the statement may still be true (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Automation and its limits|automation and its limits]]).

== Reading a message ==

The same order of reading serves for all of these. First the place: which line, which part of
it. Then the first line of the message, which names the kind of failure. Then the detail:
what was given against what was expected, or the goal that remains with what may be used for
it.

Lean tries to carry on after an error, so that one mistake does not hide the rest of the
file. Often a definition that fails is kept with a hole where the error was, and later
results that use it are still checked:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def three : Nat := "three"

theorem t : three = three := rfl
#print axioms t
</pre>

The file gives the type mismatch shown above, and then <code>'t' depends on axioms:
[sorryAx]</code>. The theorem was accepted, but only on credit: it rests on the axiom behind
<code>sorry</code>, described in [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Holes and goals|holes and
goals]]. A file is finished when it has no errors at all, not when the results at its end
are accepted.

A refusal costs little. It changes nothing that was already accepted, and it points to one
place and one kind of fault. That is why proving in Lean can proceed by trial: a wrong guess
ends in a specific message, and the message says where to look next.
